clinicalPearls: The most common primary renal malignancy of childhood, typically presenting in preschool children around 2-5 years of age.
The usual presentation is an asymptomatic, smooth abdominal mass discovered by a parent or on routine examination, sometimes with abdominal pain, haematuria, or hypertension.
The mass characteristically does not cross the midline, in contrast to neuroblastoma.
Associated with syndromes and anomalies such as WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash, and with hemihypertrophy and aniridia; these children warrant surveillance.
Examination should be gentle, avoiding vigorous palpation of the mass because of the risk of tumour rupture.
Staging and histology (favourable versus anaplastic) guide a multimodal approach combining surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy.
Bilateral disease occurs in a minority and requires nephron-sparing strategies to preserve renal function.
The lungs are the most common site of metastatic spread, so chest imaging is part of staging.
Overall survival is high, making Wilms tumour one of the success stories of paediatric oncology.
reference.pathophysiology: Wilms tumour arises from embryonal nephrogenic (metanephric) blastema, often showing a classic triphasic pattern of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements. It is linked to abnormalities of genes involved in kidney development, including WT1, and to epigenetic changes at chromosome 11p; persistent nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions. Anaplastic histology confers a worse prognosis and greater treatment resistance.
additionalDifferentials: Clear cell sarcoma or rhabdoid tumour of the kidney
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the abdomen to define the mass and the contralateral kidney
Chest imaging to assess pulmonary metastases
Full blood count, renal and liver function, urinalysis
Assessment for inferior vena cava or renal vein tumour thrombus
redFlags: Features of tumour rupture (acute abdominal pain, distension, haemodynamic instability)
reference.prognosis: With risk-adapted multimodal therapy, most children with favourable-histology disease are cured; prognosis is worse with anaplastic histology, advanced stage, or unfavourable biological features.
pitfalls: Aggressive palpation of the abdominal mass, risking rupture
Confusing it with neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and has different markers
Missing hypertension as an associated finding
Failing to screen children with predisposing syndromes
Overlooking the contralateral kidney for bilateral disease
management: Multimodal, risk-adapted therapy combining surgery, chemotherapy and selective radiotherapy according to stage and favourable versus anaplastic histology
Radical nephrectomy with lymph node sampling as the surgical mainstay, with nephron-sparing surgery considered in bilateral or syndromic disease
Chemotherapy using agents such as vincristine, actinomycin D and, for higher-risk disease, doxorubicin, given as neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment per protocol
Radiotherapy reserved for higher-stage, anaplastic or residual disease
Gentle handling with avoidance of vigorous palpation and unplanned biopsy because of the risk of tumour rupture and upstaging
Renal ultrasound surveillance in predisposing conditions such as WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Denys-Drash, hemihypertrophy and aniridia

Long-term monitoring for relapse and treatment late effects including anthracycline cardiotoxicity and renal impairment, within a paediatric oncology multidisciplinary team and with genetic counselling where syndromic
